Reference was made
last night to orders in council P.C. 2787 and 2171, by the first of which an amount of $1,447,222.71 was advanced to the Canadian Pacific Railway to pay the wages of men employed in the shops, and by the other the sum of $1,000,000 was advanced to the same railway also to pay the wages of the men employed in the Shops. In both those orders in council there is reference to arrangements that have been made to maintain operations in the shops of the Canadian National Railways. I should like to know what arrangements have been made with the Canadian National Railways for the purpose of permitting the employment of their workmen in the shops.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
At the time the first order in council was passed authorizing the $1,400,000 odd in payment of the wages of the employees on the Canadian Pacific, the position of the shopmen on both railways was giving a good deal of concern, and it was felt that keeping those shops open for a short time would probably be as sound a measure of unemployment relief as the government at that time could well adopt. The Canadian National directorate did make arrangements and provide for keeping their shops open. They might 'have closed them, and a great many of their employees would then of course have come on relief. Having regard to the fact that the Canadian National Railways, receiving as they do their money from this parliament, were keeping their
Relief Act, 1933

shops open, it was the opinion of the government, in view of the situation in which the Canadian Pacific Railway found itself, that provision should be made for the loaning to the Canadian Pacific of the amount of $1,400,000 odd in order that they might keep their shops open for a similar length of time. With reference to the authorization of a further $1,000,000, that money, while authorized, has not yet been spent, as the return of the wages paid has not yet been submitted to the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The Canadian National
Railways did not get any advance from that relief fund?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Perhaps I might explain, as the hon. Minister of Labour was not then in that department. The former Minister of Labour, Senator Robertson, dealt with this matter, and under the arrangements made, the Canadian National shops were kept open on part time without a shutdown, but the Canadian Pacific Shops had been closed, and it was a question as between giving direct relief and loaning the money to keep the shops in operation for the period of time mentioned in the order in council. But the order in council was not passed until long after the expenditure had been incurred, and with the application there were filed the vouchers signed by the workmen for all the moneys thtat had been expended for actual labour, as represented in the order in council.
There is one further thing to be said. The company thought that if there was an improvement in business it would not be essential that they should get a loan, but when there was not that improvement as expected, the order in council was passed. It will be observed that the order in council is dated September 30, 1932, long after the expenditure had been incurred, the expenditure being made in the month of December, 1931.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
My question relates to
the Canadian National Railways shops. What has been done about them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
They were not dosed.
Senator Robertson made an arrangement that permitted the Canadian National shops, by staggering employment, and with partial shutdowns, to continue open, and the recital in the order in council has reference to the arrangement made by Senator Robertson, with which the present Minister of Labour was not then familiar.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
May I refer my right
hon. friend to an answer that he gave me this 
session on November 8, at page 924 of Hansard. The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Jean) had asked a question which included this:
4. Did the government make similar advances to the Canadian National Railways?
My right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, did not reply at first to that part of the question, and I asked him what about part 4 of the question, reading, "Did the government make similar advances to the Canadian National Railways?" And the Prime Minister replied:
I thank my hon. friend for bringing that to my attention. Yes, the government did make similar advances.
That is not what my right hon. friend says now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is what I wished to convey at that time, and if the hon. gentleman had so desired it could have been amplified. There were in point of fact larger advances to the Canadian National than to the Canadian Pacific, but the advances were made by not shutting the Canadian National shops down during that period. There was more employment and a lessening of unemployment by the shops continuing to remain open during that whole period under consideration. There never was a shutdown of the Canadian National shops during that period, whereas in the other case there was a shutdown.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: But any aid given to the Canadian National Railways was not taken out of this vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Oh mo, none at alll, so
far as my memory goes, except the ties, as was mentioned by the minister a few minutes ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I brought this question up
the other day, and to-night the Prime Minister leaves the impression on the committee that there was no closing down of the Canadian National shops, that there was continuous work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Not continuous work,
but not a continuous shutdown.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
There was not an absolute
shutdown in the shops at Moncton. The work was intermittent, the shops working sometimes four days a week, and so on.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
That was true all over
the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Yes. But the point I wish to make is that while the Canadian National shops were kept open in an intermittent way

Iieliej Act, 1933
for purposes of relief, the money so expended never came out of the relief money voted by this parliament; it came out of the earnings of the Canadian National Railways, and the earnings of the road not being sufficient to meet the expenses, that amount is charged up as part of the deficit of the Canadian National Railways. Now to meet that deficit we have borrowed money on which we are paying 4} or 4} per oent. While we are charging interest to the Canadian National in that regard, we are loaning money to the Canadian Pacific at no interest at all, and in order to pay the Canadian Pacific the money that was earned under that order in council we floated bonds on which we are paying 41 or 4| per cent interest. I claim that it is not fair. It is not treating the Canadian National system right, and especially the Atlantic section, which during last year in the reduction of operating expenses was cut down to the expenditure of one-half of the whole difference between 1931 and 1932, as compared with the total mileage of the Canadian National railways throughout Canada. If we are going to furnish money to the Can* adian Pacific without charge, and we are going to say to the Canadian National, "Keep your shoips open for a certain number of days in the week or a certain number of days in the month," and then charge that expenditure up as part of the deficit of the Canadian National and make them pay interest on it at 4J per cent, I claim that we are not dealing fairly with the Canadian National.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The only difficulty about the hon. gentleman's observations is that they happen to be inaccurate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: They are not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is the only difficulty, and I think I can satisfy him on that point- even the hon. gentleman himself. In 1931 there was a surplus of revenue over expenses on the Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Not on the Atlantic division.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Excuse me-on the system as reported; and the operating expenses include charges for the keeping open of the shops. The surplus was approximately $2,000,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: How much?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
$2,000,000. In 1932 there was also a surplus of approximately $5,000,000. So that no part of the deficit paid by this parliament had reference in any way, shape or form, directly or indirectly, to the operating expenses in which were included charges for
the keeping open of the shops. The expense of keeping the shops open was charged against the operating expense of the road, from week to week and from month to month, and at the end of the year there was a surplus of income over operating expenses. The deficit was with respect to interest on capital, improvements and betterments.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I do this with some trepidation, but allow me to correct the right hon. Prime Minister. There was no surplus on the Atlantic region, and that is what I am talking about. There was a deficit of over $5,000,000 in 1931 on the Atlantic region, part of it being charged up to the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and the balance charged to operating deficit of 1931. I know whereof I speak. I rely on the records laid on the table of the house. I refer to the Atlantic region, and if the right hon. Prime Minister attempts to show there was a surplus which included the whole Canadian National railway system, he is wrong. I do not accept his word, because I know I am right. It is a matter of choosing between two facts; under the rules of the house I am not bound to accept the Prime Minister's word; knowing I am right I cannot accept it. In the year 1932 on the Atlantic region of the Canadian National railways there was a deficit of between $4,000,000 and $5,000.000. Those shops were kept open intermittently for the purpose of helping out the unemployed. At the time we were charging as a deficit the operation of the Moncton shops, we were loaning money to the Canadian Pacific Railway without interest.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I hesitate to trespass upon the time of the committee; I do not wish to waste the time of hon. members by talking about two incomparable matters. I was talking about the Canadian National railways system; the hon. member who has just taken his seat was talking about the Atlantic division. I am not talking about the Atlantic division. I have said that in the year 1931 there was a surplus of 82,000,000 on the operation of the Canadian National system. That is all I am concerned about. I could point out a dozen places where there were deficits in the Canadian National system, but at this time I have simply stated that there was a surplus of revenue over expenses. That is all I have to say.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I have more than that to say. The Prime Minister should know, and I am sure he does, that the Atlantic region, the old Intercolonial, the shops' of which are at Moncton, is not under the Canadian National railway system. Their accounts are
Reliej Act, 1933

kept separately. The Canadian National directors are authorized by order in council to manage the road. As I said the other day, the Atlantic section represents a bond between the maritime and the central provinces which was arranged at the time of confederation. All governments have religiously safeguarded the status of the old Intercolonial by saying, through order in council, that the members of the directorate of the Canadian National system on behalf of the government of Canada shall manage the road, shall keep the accounts separate and submit them to parliament. Under that arrangement the Atlantic region has had a deficit during the last five or six years. Therefore I submit the Prime Minister's argument does not hold water.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I spoke a week or so ago concerning a matter which has just been mentioned. I addressed the Minister of Railways with regard to men employed at the railway shops as the result of a grant given by the government to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have in my possession a couple of letters concerning this important point. Some of the men employed in the shops of the Canadian Pacific Railway claim they have not received the amount of work they should have received as a result of the grant given by the government to the railway company. They claim the work they should have done was being done by the foremen on a monthly basis. Because the men who were employed on a monthly basis were doing a great deal of the work, those who were employed on an hourly basis did not have the opportunity for work they should have had. If such is the case it means that the advantages gained by the grant given to the Canadian Pacific have to a large extent been nullified by the action of the railway in giving work to permanent employees who, in any event, would receive their monthly cheques.
I believe the Prime Minister said to-night, as well as on a previous occasion, that some vouchers signed by the men had been presented either to the cabinet or to parliament.
I am wondering whether those vouchers will be open for inspection, so that those who today are urging that the men on an hourly basis have not been treated fairly might receive some satisfaction. Could the vouchers be looked into so that we might ascertain whether the men received the advantages which they should have had from the moneys granted by parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
There are several volumes of vouchers respecting some 8,000 employees scattered across Canada from the Atlantic to 
the Pacific. Those vouchers are filed at the Privy Council office. I shall speak to the Clerk of the Privy Council so that it may be possible for the hon. gentleman to examine them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Is this money advanced to the Canadian Pacific to keep all their shops open? Is there any specification as to what shops will be kept open? Because I know at the present time in my own city and my own constituency employees in shops are threatened with unemployment. I know that negotiations are being carried on between the city council and the company. If a million dollars was advanced to keep the shops open I suppose Quebec will have the same treatment as other places where there are shops?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: All the shops were kept open, but it was a period of time during the Christmas season. It will be observed in 1931 the work commenced some time past the middle of November and continued up to the last work day before Christmas week. The same course was followed in 1932. The agreement was-and I have every reason to believe it was earned out-that there should be no discrimination, but that all the shops should be worked for the number of days the money would permit. But it was in November and December, 1932 that it was done.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: But the moneys are to be paid in 1933?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
During the past few
days we have heard a discussion concerning relief measures in the province of Quebec. Pemsomally I do not intend to speak at length concerning points already covered by other lion, members. I am .aware that some people find fault with certain legislation which has been in force in the province of Quebec. In the province from which I come I notice the law has been administered through the efforts of the Minister of Colonization, Game and Fisheries, the Hon. Hector Laferte. I hold no brief for him or for the provincial government in this matter, but I think it is fair to say that the law has been administered by the Department of Colonization, Game and Fisheries of the province of Quebec in a fair way, and that the people in the various districts tvhere settlements have been made are satisfied. For instance in the district I have the honour to represent in this house I know

Relief Act, 1933
that some new settlements were established behind Ste. Agnes and St. Simeon in the county of Charlevoix, also the north shore of the St. Lawrence, and in places called Mille Vaches, Les Escoumains, Canitons Latour and Laval and at Manikuagan. I have here the whole report of the Department of Colonization of the province of Quebec for the year 1932 and it is stated at page 88 that 71 families have been settled in one district and 44 the other.
But, Mr. Chairman, coming back to this movement, as was stated this afternoon by the hon. member for Kamouraska, while the government may claim this policy as its own, nevertheless I think it is not the policy of this government; it is not the Gordon scheme as we might call it, because long before this government ever had a back to the land policy we in the province of Quebec, the government that is to-day administering the affairs of that province, the Taschereau government, had started this movement of colonization.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
My hon. friend the
Postmaster General says "hear, hear." I know myself that since I have had the honour to represent the district I do represent in this house, on the river Outarde near Outarde falls great districts were settled. Families were brought from Other parts of the province of Quebec, where there are good lands, and people were established there through the efforts of the provincial government as far back as 1926 to 1930. Therefore, I think the adoption of this back to the land policy by the government in Ottawa is due to the example and the good work of the government of the province of Quebec.
While on this subject I would like to say a word with respect to the hon. Postmaster General. I want to pay a tribute to him-* for once we can agree: I can say that he has done some good, because in one of the districts I have just mentioned there was a new place called St. Isidore le Laboureur, behind St. Simeon, for which a post office and mail service was requested. I asked the Post Office Department ito grant this favour to this new settlement, and I have received confirmation of the success of my efforts in obtaining the post office and mail service through the Postmaster General. I think that is a desirable thing he has done in helping these people, giving them the services necessary to make their settlement attractive. I think also, Mr. Chairman, it is a good way to make
these people favourable and to minimize the evils for which this government have been responsible since they have been at the head of affairs in this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: This is not my birthday!

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
There is one other point to which I wish to draw the attention of the acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization. The hon. member for Kamouraska this afternoon mentioned that last night the minister said that through the efforts of his department people to the number of 100,000 or more have been attracted and brought in to settle in these different places. With the hon. member for Kamouraska I take exception to that statement as indicating the number of people who have been settled in these various places. I have mentioned a few settlements in the district I have the honour to represent, and I think it would be well for the minister to advise the committee in detail respecting the other districts of Quebec and the other provinces of Canada in which people to the extent of 100,000 have been settled through the efforts of this government. I express the opinion that if a lot of people have been settled on the land it is due not so much to the policy adopted by this administration as to the policy initiated by the government of Quebec, and I dare say that in Ontario and elsewhere they may have had in effect a similar scheme long before the federal government started its activities along that line.
I think also that the remarks made by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) should receive the careful attention of the minister. He said that only heads of families are entitled to the benefit of this plan. The sons of farmers in our province who are qualified to settle on land in these new districts ought to be encouraged just as much as heads of families, because it would mean that people would be encouraged to stay in our province to the benefit not only of the province of Quebec but of the whole of Canada.
There is also the point brought up by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) as to the classification of people who ought to go on the land. I agree with the remarks made by some hon. members this afternoon that it is better to attract to the land or keep on the land those who are accustomed to country life than men taken from the slums of cities where they have been for a good many years, idle maybe, people who for a long time have had no contact with the land and who therefore cannot have the same energy and courage to start anew, especially if they are advanced in age.
Relief Act, 1933

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: We do not take that class of people at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I say that the efforts
of this government and of the provincial governments should be directed to the settlement of the sons of agricultural families. In the report published this year by the Department of Trade and Commerce at page 184, it is stated that only heads of families can benefit from such measures. I take issue with the department on that point. I think the sons of farmers in the various provinces ought to be encouraged to avail themselves of the benefit of this back to the land scheme rather than people in the cities. And I think they ought to be encouraged as much as heads of families. I know in my own district there are many people who would be willing to take advantage of such a scheme. I think, Mr. Chairman, that this government is not entitled to take the full share of credit for what has been done, because it could not have been done without the assistance of the provincial government, which has indicated where the settlement should take place. And as I have said, the provincial government was away ahead of this administration in adopting the back to the land movement.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the present moment is an appropriate one for the minister to give us some information concerning the unemployment insurance proposals. I know he is straining at the leash and yearning to give us out of his wealth of experience and knowledge and ability a statement on the matter. He was present at the conference with the provinces and therefore is in a position to inform us in regard to this very important subject. The public will not be satisfied with any mere evasion of the subject. They had reason to believe that action would be taken on this matter, but the session is going on and I do not know of any other occasion when this question could be brought up. I think that in considering the question of relief it is quite appropriate for the minister to give us the fullest possible information on the prospects of having unemployment insurance put. into effect in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Dealing first with the observations of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, let me say at once that there is no intention, and I hope there never will be, of trying to take credit away from the province of Quebec with respect to colonization. If the work carried on by the province of Quebec along these lines in the past needed

defence, I defended them in the house against the impeachment of the hon. member for Temiscouata. Anyone who have even casual knowledge of the history of the development of Canada should not be slow to commend the actions of the successive governments of the province of Quebec even before confederation, and in fact almost since the beginning of settlement, along this line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: If the minister would allow me, I think he should make a distinction between colonization and the back to the land movement. I think several hon. members have become confused. There are two systems in Quebec, but colonization before confederation has nothing whatever to do with the back to the land movement.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I was endeavouring to reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, who referred-and I think very properly-to colonization and the back to the land movement. So far as I am concerned I see very little difference between the two, but perhaps my hon. friend may see some refinements that I am unable to distinguish. There is no question of who is to get credit for this or that. If I may use the w'ord, Mr. Chairman, I do not care a continental who gets the credit so long as we either lead the way or supplement the efforts of those leading the way in order that the desired object may be attained, that is, that those who are ready and willing and desirable may take full advantage of this opportunity to make themselves independent and selfsustaining. If any success has attended the efforts of this government, in conjunction with the provinces and the railway companies; if any credit is due anyone with respect to any assistance this government has been able to give, I will hand that credit to anyone. I will give it to the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay. He can take it to himself with my blessing; it will be his very own, so long as we do what we are hoping to do. This business of taking credit one way or the other at a time like this does not give me any great concern.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Did the minister say I had impeached the province of Quebec? Were those the words he used?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I do not know that I can recall my exact words, but in substance I said the hon. member for Temiscouata had criticized the colonization efforts of the government of the province of Quebec. So far as I know the efforts of that government deserve credit, and my contact with their officials

Relief Act, 1933
certainly has been pleasant and profitable. I have found them desirous of accomplishing what has been my objective, and probably they had that end in view long before I came into public life.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a
question of privilege. I am sorry to interrupt the minister, but he said he had to defend the province of Quebec against the impeachment of the hon. member for Temiscouata. Those were his words; I was looking at pictures but listening to his speech, and my understanding is corroborated by those about me on this side of the house. Is it fair for a minister of the crown to use such language, especially after I repeated my complaints this afternoon? I was not complaining of the government of Quebec; I did not say a word against the government, against the provincial minister or against my hon. friend. Is it fair to give a false interpretation to my words? I ask the minister to withdraw his reference to the impeachment of the province of Quebec by the hon. member for Temiscouata; it would be only fair.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I am quite content to let the words of the hon. member for Temiscouata, as they will be revealed in the pages of Hansard, speak for themselves. If I used words which were not exactly his I can only say that of course my memory is not so good that I can follow him exactly. Certainly I gathered from his remarks to-day and a few days ago that he roundly condemned the administration of the colonization department of the province of Quebec.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: By certain employees.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The government takes responsibility for its officials, of course. The hon. member went so far as to say that the colonists who were sent out by the government had to eat grass and roots and so on, and I believe he even said they lived like swine. I do not come in contact with the provincial colonization men and I have nothing to do with provincial policies in Quebec, but I do know that this department is in touch with our committee, which consists of the representatives of the colonization departments of the railways, of our department and of the Quebec department. From my observations and from what I can gather I cannot conceive that those men would be parties to a colonization effort such as has been described by the hon. member for Temiscouata.
With regard to the situation in my hon. friend's own constituency I can only say that under the assisted plan we have placed only
two settlers in that county, and I have been instructed by the head of the colonization department of the Canadian National Railways that from both of these settlers he recently received communications stating that they were getting along well, that they were very happy to be located where they are, and so on. Our locations are almost entirely in the Abitibi and Timiskaming district, and I have lengthy reports concerning the way those settlers are getting on. There is throughout a spirit of satisfaction with the locations upon which they are placed and with the conditions under which they are living, and a feeling of optimism prevails amongst these settlers. There were not housed together in buildings, men, women and children huddled together, as suggested. The hon. member for Temiscouata was not in his place this afternoon when I explained that the heads of families preceded the families. They were taken care of, their locations were picked out in a fertile section of the country adjacent to the mining areas of northwestern Quebec, and their families followed after them. A representative of the Canadian National Railways, because it is the Canadian National that runs through that country, has made many trips visiting these people. Their churches are being built and the general atmosphere is one of optimism.
I will not delay the committee by reading all the communications I have received, or even a number of them, from that locality, but I can assure hon. members that what I say is correct with respect not only to the feeling that exists amongst these settlers but with respect to their confidence in the future. Hon. members who represent city constituencies must bear in mind that it is difficult for them, if they have not been around a great mining area like northwestern Quebec and parts of northern Ontario, to visualize the opportunities that are there for the Canadian people. It is a wonderful thing for the country that we have such places in these parts of Canada. It is quite true that the farmers there are experiencing difficulties, just as the farmers throughout the world are; but they have excellent locations and their homes are largely unencumbered, inasmuch as their locations were crown lands; and while across the Ontario boundary the settlement is older than it is in Quebec, nevertheless wonderful strides are being made in the colonization of that country. I do not say this purely because the hon. member for Temiscouata doubts the soundness of the program that is being contributed to by the federal government; I state it merely as a fact, so that the committee will get a picture of the movement of these settlers

Since I have been a member of this house I have refrained from quoting from newspapers, but if I may be pardoned for doing so on this occasion, I would read what the deputy minister of the colonization, game and fisheries department of Quebec had to say with reference to a visit to that area:
In an interview accorded a Chronicle-Telegraph representative this morning, Deputy Minister L. A. Richard of the Provincial Colonization, Game and Fisheries Department, expressed his amazement at the unbounded enthusiasm which he had personally witnessed amongst the "back to the land colonists," who were only a few weeks ago settled on arable and wooded lots in the Temiskaming district.
Mr. Richard, who accompanied his minister, Hon. Hector Laferte, and a number of rail-waymen and prominent citizens, has just returned from a visit to the newly formed settlement, not far from the banks of the "Lonely River," where these hardy sons and daughters of Quebec are going to wrest a home and comfortable living from mother earth who they deserted in their more prosperous days, but who has received them back again in the days of their adversity.
In prefacing his interview, Mr. Richard explained that when these heads of families were picked for the great experiment, it was with the knowledge that they were former farmers, and all of them knew a smattering of carpentry, that is, they knew how to put together a log cabin.
"The visit to these settlers of ours was a revelation to me," said the Deputy Minister. "I had been told they were satisfied, but I was not prepared to see all of them bubbling over with unbounded enthusiasm. They are! Everyone of them! There wasn't a kick anywhere, and I surely thought there might be, as they had been placed on the land so late in the year.
"I talked with many of them and their speech was just the same. Thankfulness that at last after many weary months of wrestling with the wolf at the door, they were their own masters. Living in houses they had built themselves. Their fate in their own hands; their immediate wants provided for by a beneficent government, or rather I should say beneficent federal, provincial and municipal governments. No taxes to pay; no irate landlords demanding their pounds of flesh; soil which will grow almost anything; brooks and streams teeming with all kinds of fish in season, also a pure water supply brought from the surrounding hills; a moose perhaps, and partridge and hares running around waiting to be bagged and put in the larder."
I am sure this part of the interview will be quite interesting to the hon. member for Temiscouata, the hon. member for Charle-voixnSaguenay and, I might almost venture to suggest, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni:
This picture is not exaggerated! These people are happy, and you would have thought so too if you had seen about a thousand of them, men, women and children, as they attended open air mass on Sunday last, and witnessed the first marriage in the settlement
LMr. Gordon.]
which by the way is to be called St. Monica de Rollet, after the wife of Louis Hebert, the first Canadian settler. Incidentally Hon. Mr. Laferte gave the bride away and kissed her heartily.
I have many such communications from these settlers. Now, I do not think they will be one hundred per cent successes; they never have been in the past. We do look forward however to a considerable and substantial permanent settlement, although there will unquestionably be disappointments.
With reference to the question asked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I do not think the measure now before the house affords the proper opportunity to discuss the matter of unemployment insurance, which is a very broad one. Many countries in the world have attempted some sort of unemployment insurance, and many private concerns have endeavoured to fashion a plan of some kind that would1 take up the slack in times when industry had failed to give that job security which is so essential to the workers in industrial centres. Plans have been instituted1 in certain countries in Europe, and in the United States industries have set up schemes-such industries as the General Electric Company-in connection with the question. The whole question of unemployment insurance is one of great complexity. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I take it, would like to know whether a measure of that kind will be brought before the house this session. I can tell him it will not. No government would be justified in hurriedly embarking on a project the success of which would be founded perhaps in very large measure upon a careful study of the various factors that enter into the consideration of it.
The matter is under consideration by the government, as it is unquestionably under consideration by many public bodies, and it is hoped that some solution will be found in order to give to the workers that security during seasonal unemployment, or unemployment for any other reason, which many people think -the workers should enjoy. No government would embark hurriedly on a plan of that sort without having canvassed every possibility of success or failure. We had to take into consideration the necessity of establishing it upon a firm foundation so that it would not meet with disaster during the course of its operation. I think we were adopting a wise course with respect to so important a subject.

In other words the preamble deals entirely with high grade government securities. But the executory portion of the order in council deals with all securities. I imagine that under this order in council the banks, in their reports, were entitled to value Brazilian, Nickel, Canadian Pacific and all other common stocks as of their value on August 31, 1931, although as a matter of fact, when this order in council was passed, these stocks had fallen considerably. To-day they are considerably lower in value on the security markets of the world than they were at that time. It seems to me that to a considerable extent this was giving government assistance to the banks. It was at least supporting their credit to a considerable extent and permitting them to make reports of their securities at other than their real value on the ordinary security market.
Listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) I noticed that the report of the committee of the legislature of Manitoba called attention to the fact that the government had permitted a revaluation of securities held by insurance companies. Apparently they were not aware that the banks had been permitted to revalue their securities. I suggest that if the savings bank of Manitoba had been permitted the same valuation of its securities as the chartered banks of Canada were, there might have been a chance of saving it. I suppose, Mr. Chairman, it is within the knowledge of this committee that the savings office of Manitoba was not a bank. The observations to which we have just listened would leave the conclusion in the

Relief Act, 1933
minds of the committee that it was a savings bank. The province of Manitoba has no authority to conduct a bank. It has a savings office, as has the province of Ontario. And there are grave doubts in the minds of many as to whether or not the provinces have power at all to conduct the form of office they were conducting, which consisted in receiving from the people deposits withdrawable by cheque. It has been contended, and is still contended by eminent legal authorities, that neither province has a legal right to engage in that business. The word "bank" is not used for that very reason; "savings office," and not "savings bank," is the term used. If they were banks they would come within the provisions of the Bank Act; they have sought no authority from this parliament to open savings banks. There would be no reason why the province of Ontario or the province of Manitoba, if they so desired, should not obtain from this parliament the right to conduct a bank, and if they did they would be subject to the requirements of the Bank Act with respect to paid-up capital, the obtaining of a proper and appropriate directorate, and the conduct of business under inspection.
The moneys that were deposited in the savings offices at Winnipeg and other points in Manitoba aggregated the sum of $12,000,000 or more. In the month of January the depositors began to withdraw their money. As the province had no money with which to meet these demands-and nothing more clearly indicates what the science of banking really requires than this very transaction- they were called upon to secure the money from some source. They borrowed it from a chartered bank and gave as security for the loan thus obtained the bonds of the Dominion of Canada in which they had invested a portion of the depositors' money. As I understand the science of banking-my knowledge is limited-it consists in the maintenance of an equilibrium between time deposits and time loans on the one hand and demand deposits and demand loans on the other. If a bank ties up in time loans money required to meet its demand deposits it becomes insolvent. If it ties up its assets in time loans to an extent that makes it impossible for it to meet the cheques of its depositors, you have exactly the situation they had in the United States of America the week before last. In that country four thousand banks failed during the last few months. Why? Because they had taken deposits from people and invested the money in real estate, mortgages, and other assets
which could not be sold, and there was therefore no money with which the demands of the depositors could be met; being unable to pay they closed their doors and went into liquidation.
The province of Manitoba in the month of January had no money in its till-that is admitted. But it was able to borrow a certain sum of money from the Canadian Bank of Commerce by pledging its Dominon of Canada bonds, under an option agreement whereby the bank was entitled for a given time to buy them at a figure if the bank so desired. That was the source of cash for the province of Manitoba to put into its till to meet the demands of its depositors. When the run on the savings office began-and the committee of the legislative assembly reported that suspicion and rumour were largely responsible for it; I am not going to discuss that-they had to get money somewhere. Being unable to get further money from the banks they had nothing but their own I.O.U.'s. Objection is taken to the use of that term by me, but it is exactly what the security was-I.O.U.'s which could not be sold for the purpose of providing cash to meet the cheque demands of the depositors. Then it was that the chartered banks and the province made the arrangement to which I refer. That arrangement not being to the satisfaction of the banks, they said: "We will not do this with the security you offer us, because someone has to provide as much as $12,000,000, possibly the -whole of it within the next thirty days"-because although the province claim they were entitled to notice of withdrawals, I think the maximum was thirty days and perhaps in some cases the term was as low as ten days. So that $12,000,000 was the possible amount that the banks might have to supply, and the banks divided this among themselves rateably on the basis of their business in -the city of Winnipeg, each assuming its proportion of responsibility to meet the demands of the depositors. They said: "We will do this only on one condition, namely that the Dominion government give its guarantee." The banks had $12,000,000 and more of province of Manitoba securities, bonds and treasury bills, and with the guarantee of the dominion, they assumed the responsibility of meeting on demand the cheques of any depositors in the savings offices of Manitoba. I will not further traverse that matter.

a temporary necessity that arose by reason of a complete demoralization of the world's markets, but there was no change in the real value of the securities that were held, they being, as I have said, the class of securities that banks purchase in order to take care of conditions which, in the wisdom of those who manage them, may at any time arise. It is common knowledge that difficulties have arisen in some of the great countries of the world. Corporations have drawn their cheques to meet their pay-rolls and limitations have been placed upon the amount that might be drawn; so much has been set as the maximum for each workman, and so much as the maximum for each executive. Even great insurance companies have had to apply limitations and restrictions as to the payment of cash surrender values and the making of loans on policies. This action was taken to prevent any possible disruption or disorganization of our banking system and to maintain the confidence of the depositors so that, with few exceptions, there were no large withdrawals from the banks, and the integrity of our institutions has been maintained.

If that were the case, Canadian Pacific stock, which was one of the securities they were permitted to value as of its market value on August 31 or its book value, most assuredly would be valued in the October statement at more than its real value in the markets of the world on that date. I hope if I am making any mis-statements I will be corrected, because I do not want to exaggerate the situation in any way or to say anything that is not correct. I would assume

That was one of the points I was endeavouring to make. Whether or not the banks took advantage of this order in council I am unable to say, but it permitted them to make their reports for the months of September, October, November and December of 1931, and their annual report for that year, as well as their reports for the following months until March, 1932, showing the value of their securities on the basis set out in this order in council. Then I will say that a considerable proportion, if my right hon. friend will agree to that, was invested in provincial and federal government securities because, we are told, these were liquid. I do not know that we ever had a better example of when they were not liquid than in the case we have been discussing. I suppose the same observation could be made with justice in respect to the banks in the United States which unfortunately have had to close. A large number of banks, under the state banking laws, were permitted to value their securities at other than the market value, but apparently that was not sufficient to save them from the liquidation which resulted, which forced a large number of banks in that country to close their doors.
I very much regret that I used the word "bank" with reference to the Manitoba savings office. I quite understand that there is some discussion as to whether or not provinces have the right to call these institutions banks, but I am not particularly concerned with that. This was an institution which held the savings of the people and, as such, it was entitled to whatever protection could be afforded. Whether or not it could be properly called a bank or an office is not material to the discussion; the fact that it was an office and not a bank should not be made an excuse for not extending to it all the assistance this government could give.

I think not, because that was not the phase of it with which we felt we had authority to deal. That was purely a banking transaction, between the bank and its customers, and to interfere with the bank's transaction of business would involve on the part of the country the examination of the various accounts of individuals, which we declined under any circumstances to do or to accept the responsibility for. And it was because of difficulties that arose by reason of the very circumstances to which the former Minister of Trade and Commerce has alluded that I for one did not feel, and I do not yet think, that it was desirable for the dominion to become responsible in the way of taking over the savings offices in Manitoba. To take them over and to become responsible for cash and to deal with customers was not the business of the country. What we did was to use the collective credit of the people of Canada to make certain that over 40,000 depositors in the province of Manitoba, having aggregate savings of 812,000,000, should not lose those savings or should not be delayed in receiving their money by reason of the fact that the money they had paid in had been invested in something that could not be realized upon. That is the short way of putting it. In other words, you could not realize on a mortgage on real estate for the purpose of meeting a cheque; and when you substituted, for the money you took, a mortgage and then exchanged the mortgage for a treasury bill with the promise to pay, and could not sell that, you were no better off, because your treasury was empty of cash in either event; and because it was empty of cash, the situation developed as I have indicated.
I think, without trespassing further on the time of the committee, that what we endeavoured to do we succeeded in doing, namely, preventing shall I say suspicion and distrust undermining the confidence of the Canadian people in their financial institutions, so that they might be tempted to withdraw their money and hoard it, as has been done in other countries of the world during the great depression through which we are passing. It is a matter of satisfaction and for that reason I felt especially pleased with what was said yesterday by the leader of the opposition regarding the condition of this country as compared with other countries, because, whatever else may be said, we had met the demands that were made by the depositors in our financial institutions for their money in accordance with the terms of their contract of deposit, without any hesitancy
or any request for delay or for limitation of the amount they might receive in accordance with the balance outstanding to their credit.

I think the minister might give more information with respect to the question raised by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi as 'to what transpired at the dominion-provincial conference in regard to unemployment insurance. It is a very important question, especially when we are discussing unemployment relief measures, and it is one that has been the subject of debate in this house for several years. I can recall its being submitted to the industrial relationships committee on two occasions, after which the provinces were canvassed to see what view they took of the matter. I think the files of the department will show that at least four of the provinces agreed to participate in a conference looking to the establishment of an unemployment insurance scheme in Canada. Certainly the Prime Minister of Canada gave the workers of the country hope, on April 29, 1931, that there would be introduced in this house an unemployment insurance scheme. His words are to be found at page 1103 of Hansard of April 29, 1931. After stating what was first to be considered with regard to the number of those who would come under the scheme, and so forth, he said:
I propose, if we are spared as a government and as individuals, that the information we will have before our term of office is ended shall be crystallized into the form of legislative proposals to be submitted to this house.
I recall the large headlines that were carried in the newspapers of the country, to the effect that the government intended to introduce an unemployment insurance scheme in the House of Commons, and I also recall many of the labour men expressing the hope that it would come into existence at an early date. I realize of course that it was necessary to discuss the matter with the provinces, and that conference was called and met here not very long ago.
